title: Putting a business idea into practice

tips.title: Break-even is fixed costs over contribution
tips.body: Fixed costs are the **bill**; contribution (price minus variable cost per unit) is what each sale **chips in** towards it. Break-even asks how many chips pay the bill: fixed costs ÷ contribution. If you divided by the price instead, you forgot that every sale first has to pay for its own materials.

tips.title: Own it, owe it, or share it
tips.body: Every source of finance on the specification is one of three. Money the business **owns**: personal savings, retained profit. Money it **owes**: overdraft, trade credit, loans. Money raised by **sharing** the business: share capital, venture capital. Crowdfunding can be any of the three, depending on what the backers are promised.

tips.title: Closing walks across to opening
tips.body: In a cash-flow forecast the **closing balance** of one month walks across to become the **opening balance** of the next, never the other way. Work down each column (inflows, outflows, net cash flow, closing balance), then carry the closing figure across. Most lost marks in this topic are a balance that did not walk.

tips.title: Cash is not profit
tips.body: A profitable business can still run out of cash if customers pay late or stock is bought in advance. A cash-flow question is about **timing**; a profit question is about the whole period. Read which one is being asked.

tips.title: Margin of safety is a distance
tips.body: It is current sales **minus** break-even sales: how far output could fall before a loss. Give it in units or in pounds of sales, not as a percentage unless asked.

tips.title: Find the contribution first
tips.body: Work out **price minus variable cost per unit** and write it down before touching the break-even formula. Everything else divides by it — break-even, margin of safety, the lot — so one number computed once, carefully, protects every answer that follows it.

why.matters: An idea becomes a business the moment money starts moving, and money moves in two directions. This topic gives you the four sums that decide whether a business lives: revenue against costs (**profit**), how many you must sell before you make anything at all (**break-even**), whether the cash arrives before the bills do (**cash flow**), and where the money to start comes from. Profitable businesses close because of the third one, which is why cash gets a section of its own.

examples.title: The school disco
examples.body:
The hall costs **£150** whether 20 people come or 200: a fixed cost. Every ticket includes a drink that costs **£1**: a variable cost. Tickets are **£4**, so each one contributes **£3** towards the hall, and break-even is £150 ÷ £3 = **50 tickets**.

Sell 120 and the margin of safety is 70 tickets, and the profit is 120 × £3 − £150 = **£210**. Every decision the organisers make — a cheaper hall, a dearer ticket, no free drink — moves that 50 up or down.

visual.alt: A break-even chart for the disco: a revenue line from the origin at four pounds a ticket, a total costs line starting at the hundred and fifty pound hall hire and rising a pound a ticket, crossing at fifty tickets, with a hundred and twenty tickets marked to the right

examples.title: Profitable and broke
examples.body:
A window cleaner does **£2,000** of work in January and her costs for the month are **£800**: a profit of **£1,200**. But her customers pay 30 days later, so in January nothing comes in and £800 goes out. She started with **£1,000**, so she ends January with **£200** — and if the van needs a £300 repair she cannot pay for it, in a profitable month.

February is fine: January's £2,000 arrives. Cash is about **when** money moves; profit is about how much.

visual.alt: A two-month cash-flow forecast: January has nothing in and eight hundred out, taking the balance from a thousand to two hundred, and February's two thousand of receipts takes it to fourteen hundred

examples.title: Owe it or share it
examples.body:
A start-up needs **£10,000**. A bank loan means paying back **£11,500** over three years: **£1,500** of interest, **15%** of what was borrowed, and then the business is the owner's again.

An investor who puts in £10,000 for a **20%** share costs nothing now and never has to be repaid — but a fifth of every future profit is theirs for as long as the business exists, and they get a say. Neither is cheaper. They cost different things, and the case study tells you which the owner can afford.

visual.alt: A table comparing a ten thousand pound bank loan, repaid with fifteen per cent interest and still owed if the business fails, against an investor taking a twenty per cent share who is never repaid but takes a fifth of every profit

steps.title: Aims and objectives: what the business is for
steps.body:
An **aim** is what the business wants to achieve overall; an **objective** is a measurable target on the way to it. *Be the best-known bakery in town* is an aim; *sell 500 loaves a week by December* is an objective.

The specification splits objectives into two kinds.

**Financial**: survival, profit, sales, market share, financial security.

**Non-financial**: social objectives, personal satisfaction, challenge, independence and control.

Why they differ between businesses: a start-up's first objective is usually **survival**, because most new businesses fail in their first years. An established business aims for profit or market share. A social enterprise puts a community objective first. And many small businesses exist because the owner wanted to be their own boss, so independence matters more to them than growth.

rows: sell 500 a week; 10% of local market
enough saved to survive a bad month
employ people the job market overlooks
props.title: Business objectives on the specification

visuals.alt: A table of financial and non-financial objectives with an example of each

check.prompt: Which objective is most likely to come first for a business in its first year?
check.solution: Most new businesses fail early, so simply staying in business is the first hurdle. Market share and financial security come later.
options: Financial security
Challenge
Survival
Market share

steps.title: Revenue, costs and profit
steps.body:
Three quantities, three formulas, and they are the ones the exam uses:

$$\text{Revenue} = \text{price} \times \text{quantity sold}$$

$$\text{Total costs} = \text{fixed costs} + \text{variable costs}$$

$$\text{Profit} = \text{revenue} - \text{total costs}$$

**Fixed costs** do not change with output: rent, salaries, insurance, loan repayments. **Variable costs** rise with every unit made: materials, packaging, the electricity that runs the machines.

If profit comes out negative, the business has made a **loss**.

The word to be careful with is *revenue*. It is the money that comes in from sales, before any costs are taken off. Students lose marks by calling it profit.

visuals.alt: A card with the three formulas: revenue is price times quantity, total costs are fixed plus variable, profit is revenue minus total costs

check.prompt: A shop sells 150 T-shirts at £12 each. Calculate its revenue.

steps.title: A month in a small bakery
steps.body: Every profit question is the same three lines in the same order: revenue, total costs, then the difference. Write each line, with its label, and the method marks are safe even if the arithmetic slips.

visuals.problem: Priya's bakery: 800 loaves at £2.50; rent and wages £1200; ingredients £0.90 a loaf

steps.note: A profit, but a small one: £80 on £2000 of sales

check.prompt: Priya sells loaves at £2.50 each, pays £1200 a month in rent and wages, and spends £0.90 on ingredients per loaf. What would her profit be in a month when she sold 900 loaves?
check.solution: Revenue $= 2.50 \times 900 = 2250$. Variable $= 0.90 \times 900 = 810$. Total costs $= 1200 + 810 = 2010$. Profit $= 2250 - 2010 = £240$. Every extra loaf adds £1.60.

steps.title: Break-even: the sales that cover the costs
steps.body:
The **break-even level of output** is the number of units a business must sell for revenue to equal total costs: no profit, no loss.

$$\text{Break-even output} = \dfrac{\text{fixed costs}}{\text{price} - \text{variable cost per unit}}$$

The bottom of the fraction, price minus variable cost, is what each sale **contributes** towards the fixed costs. Sell at £25 with a variable cost of £10, and every sale puts £15 towards the rent. With £6000 of fixed costs, that takes $6000 \div 15 = 400$ sales.

On the chart, revenue is a straight line from the origin and total costs is a straight line that starts at the fixed costs. Where they cross is break-even. Left of it, costs are above revenue: a loss. Right of it, revenue is above costs: profit.

visuals.alt: A break-even chart: a revenue line from the origin, a total costs line starting at 6000, a dashed fixed costs line at 6000, and the crossing point marked at 400 units

check.prompt: Fixed costs are £3000, the price is £20 and the variable cost per unit is £8. Calculate the break-even output.

steps.title: Reading the chart: margin of safety and what moves the lines
steps.body:
**Margin of safety** is how far actual sales are above break-even:

$$\text{Margin of safety} = \text{actual output} - \text{break-even output}$$

It is the fall in sales the business could survive before making a loss. A margin of 250 units on 650 sales is comfortable; a margin of 10 is living on the edge.

The chart also shows what changes do. A **price rise** steepens the revenue line, so it crosses the cost line sooner: break-even falls. A **rise in variable costs** steepens the total cost line: break-even rises. A **rise in fixed costs** lifts the whole cost line: break-even rises. The exam asks these as *what happens to break-even if...*, and the answer is always in the formula.

visuals.alt: The same break-even chart with actual output of 650 units marked to the right of the 400-unit break-even point, showing the margin of safety

steps.text: Or: 250 units above break-even, each contributing £15: $250 \times 15 = £3750$
steps.note: Same answer both ways, which is a good check

check.prompt: Break-even is 400 units. Fixed costs rise from £6000 to £7500 with price £25 and variable cost £10 unchanged. Calculate the new break-even output.
check.solution: $7500 \div (25 - 10) = 7500 \div 15 = 500$ units. Higher fixed costs need more sales to cover them.

steps.title: Cash is not profit
steps.body:
**Cash** is the money actually in the bank. A business needs it every day: to pay suppliers, wages, rent and bills when they fall due. Run out of cash and the business cannot pay, and a business that cannot pay its debts is **insolvent** and can be closed, however profitable it looks on paper.

That last phrase is the point. **Profit** is revenue minus costs over a period. **Cash flow** is money in and money out, with its timing. They differ because:

- Customers may pay weeks after the sale, but suppliers want paying now.
- Buying a van or a machine takes all the cash at once, but the profit figure spreads the cost over years.
- Stock bought and not yet sold has used cash but earned nothing yet.

More new businesses fail from running out of cash than from making a loss.

visuals.problem: Profitable and broke in the same month

steps.text: Leo takes a £6000 furniture order in March: £2000 of timber, £1500 of labour, £2500 profit when delivered
He pays for the timber and the labour in March. The customer pays on delivery in May
March: cash out £3500, cash in £0. The bank balance falls by £3500 and nothing comes back until May
The order is profitable. The business is still short of cash in March

check.prompt: Which of these is the best reason a profitable business might be unable to pay a bill on time?
check.solution: Profit is about totals; cash is about timing. If money comes in after it has to go out, the business can be profitable and still have nothing in the account on the day a bill is due.
options: Its revenue for the year is lower than its total costs for the year
Customers pay later than the business has to pay its suppliers
It has made a loss over the year, so there is no money in the bank
It has no fixed costs, so it has nothing to pay the bill with

steps.title: The cash-flow forecast
steps.body:
A **cash-flow forecast** predicts the money in and out each month, so a shortage can be seen coming and an overdraft (the bank letting the account go below zero, covered in the next step) arranged before the bill arrives. Two formulas matter, and they link the four lines of the table — inflows, outflows, net cash flow, balance:

$$\text{Net cash flow} = \text{total inflows} - \text{total outflows}$$

$$\text{Closing balance} = \text{opening balance} + \text{net cash flow}$$

The **closing balance** of one month is the **opening balance** of the next. That link is where the marks are lost: work down each column, then carry the closing figure across.

visuals.alt: A three-month cash-flow forecast with inflows, outflows, net cash flow, opening balance and closing balance, showing the closing balance carried forward as the next month's opening balance

steps.text: A negative closing balance in February: the business needs an overdraft of at least £700 that month
March opens at $-700$; net $= 1800$; closing $= £1100$. The shortage was temporary, which the forecast showed in advance
steps.note: The forecast's job is to reveal February before it happens

check.prompt: A business has an opening balance of £3000, inflows of £5000 and outflows of £6500 in a month. Calculate the closing balance.

steps.title: Where the money comes from
steps.body:
**Short-term** finance covers a cash shortage for weeks or months:

- **Overdraft**: the bank lets the account go below zero, up to a limit. Flexible, but interest is charged daily and the rate is high.
- **Trade credit**: a supplier lets the business pay 30 or 60 days after delivery. Free, if paid on time.

**Long-term** finance pays for starting up or growing:

- **Personal savings**: no interest and no loss of control, but limited, and the owner's own money is at risk.
- **Loans**: a fixed sum repaid with interest over years. Keeps ownership, but repayments are due whatever happens.
- **Retained profit**: profit kept in the business rather than paid out. Free, but only exists once the business is profitable.
- **Share capital**: selling shares in a company. No repayment, but the new shareholders own part of the business and its profit.
- **Venture capital**: investors who put money into risky start-ups for a share, often with advice attached.
- **Crowdfunding**: many small amounts from the public online, often in return for the product or a reward.

The choice always turns on the same question: does the owner want to **owe** money or **share** the business?

visuals.alt: A table of the sources of finance, whether each is short or long term, and the main cost of each

check.prompt: A start-up wants finance without giving away any ownership and without monthly repayments. Which source fits best?
check.solution: Savings involve no repayments and no new owners. Venture capitalists and share capital give away ownership; a loan means repayments.
options: Share capital
Personal savings
A bank loan
Venture capitalists

steps.title: Your turn: work a break-even through
steps.body: Fixed costs £4000, price £20, variable cost £12 a unit. Work the break-even output one line at a time: contribution first, then the division.

visuals.fallback: Contribution per unit is $20 - 12 = £8$. Break-even $= 4000 \div 8 = 500$ units.

check.prompt: Same business: fixed costs £4000, price £20, variable cost £12. It sells 620 units. Calculate the margin of safety.
check.solution: Break-even is 500 units. Margin of safety $= 620 - 500 = 120$ units.

steps.title: Going deeper: the questions that combine two ideas
steps.body:
Section 1.3 is where Business asks you to calculate, and the top marks go to the questions that chain two calculations or read a change off a formula.

**Interest on a loan.** $\text{Interest (\%)} = \dfrac{\text{total repayment} - \text{amount borrowed}}{\text{amount borrowed}} \times 100$. Borrow £10 000, repay £11 500: interest is $1500 \div 10\,000 \times 100 = 15\%$.

**What happens to break-even if...** Do not guess; look at the formula. Anything that makes the bottom smaller, a lower price or a higher variable cost, raises break-even. A higher fixed cost raises it. A higher price lowers it, and the follow-up point is that fewer customers may buy.

**Profitable but out of cash.** The analyse question that catches people. The answer is timing: customers pay later than suppliers demand payment, and big purchases use cash at once. The cash-flow forecast exists to show that month in advance.

**Which source of finance.** It always turns on owe or share, and on whether the business already has the cash flow to meet repayments. A proven business can borrow; a risky start-up may have to give up equity.

steps.text: A business breaks even at 400 units and sells 650. Then rent rises by £1500
New margin of safety: $650 - 500 = 150$ units, down from 250
So the rent rise has cut the cushion by 100 units. Sales now only have to fall by $150 \div 650$, about 23%, before the business makes a loss; before, they could fall by $250 \div 650$, nearly 40%
steps.note: The last line turns two numbers into a judgement

check.prompt: A business borrows £8000 and repays £9200 in total. Calculate the interest as a percentage of the amount borrowed.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Objectives**: financial (survival, profit, sales, market share, security) and non-financial (social, satisfaction, challenge, independence). A start-up's first is survival.
- **Revenue** $=$ price $\times$ quantity. **Total costs** $=$ fixed $+$ variable. **Profit** $=$ revenue $-$ total costs.
- **Break-even output** $=$ fixed costs $\div$ (price $-$ variable cost per unit). Lower price or higher costs raise it.
- **Margin of safety** $=$ actual output $-$ break-even output.
- **Cash is not profit.** Timing of payments and one-off purchases mean a profitable business can run out of cash, and running out of cash is what closes businesses.
- **Net cash flow** $=$ inflows $-$ outflows. **Closing balance** $=$ opening $+$ net cash flow, and it becomes next month's opening balance.
- **Interest** $=$ (repayment $-$ borrowed) $\div$ borrowed $\times 100$.
- **Finance**: short-term is overdraft and trade credit; long-term is savings, loans, retained profit, shares, venture capital, crowdfunding. The choice is owe or share.

visuals.alt: A card with the five formulas: break-even output, margin of safety, net cash flow, closing balance and interest

questions.prompt: A stall sells 200 cups of coffee at £3 each. Calculate its revenue.
questions.solution: Revenue $=$ price $\times$ quantity $= 3 \times 200 = £600$.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a fixed cost for a café?
questions.solution: Rent is the same every month however many coffees are sold, so it is fixed. Beans, milk and cups rise with every sale, so they are variable.
options: Paper cups
Coffee beans
Rent for the premises
Milk

questions.prompt: A business has fixed costs of £1200 a month and variable costs of £4 per unit. It makes 300 units. Calculate its total costs for the month.
questions.solution: Total costs $=$ fixed $+$ variable $= 1200 + 4 \times 300 = 1200 + 1200 = £2400$.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a non-financial objective?
questions.solution: Personal satisfaction, independence, challenge and social objectives are non-financial. Survival, profit, sales, market share and financial security are the financial ones.
options: Increasing market share
Survival in the first year
Making a profit of £20 000
Personal satisfaction from running the business

questions.prompt: A business has revenue of £8000, fixed costs of £2500 and variable costs of £3000. Calculate its profit.
questions.solution: Total costs $= 2500 + 3000 = £5500$. Profit $=$ revenue $-$ total costs $= 8000 - 5500 = £2500$.

questions.prompt: A business has fixed costs of £6000. It sells its product for £25 and the variable cost per unit is £10. Calculate the break-even level of output.
questions.solution: Break-even $=$ fixed costs $\div$ (price $-$ variable cost per unit) $= 6000 \div (25 - 10) = 6000 \div 15 = 400$ units. Each sale contributes £15 towards the £6000 of fixed costs.

questions.prompt: A business breaks even at 400 units and actually sells 650. Calculate its margin of safety.
questions.solution: Margin of safety $=$ actual output $-$ break-even output $= 650 - 400 = 250$ units. Sales could fall by 250 before it makes a loss.

questions.prompt: In one month a business has cash inflows of £9500 and cash outflows of £7200. Calculate its net cash flow.
questions.solution: Net cash flow $=$ inflows $-$ outflows $= 9500 - 7200 = £2300$.

questions.prompt: A business starts the month with an opening balance of £1500. Its net cash flow for the month is $-£2000$. Calculate its closing balance.
questions.solution: Closing balance $=$ opening balance $+$ net cash flow $= 1500 + (-2000) = -£500$. A negative closing balance means the business needs an overdraft or it cannot pay its bills.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a short-term source of finance?
questions.solution: An overdraft and trade credit are short-term: they cover a cash shortage for weeks or months. Loans, share capital, venture capital, retained profit, personal savings and crowdfunding are long-term.
options: Retained profit
An overdraft
A bank loan repaid over five years
Share capital

questions.prompt: A business has fixed costs of £6000, a variable cost of £10 per unit and sells at £25. It raises its price to £30. Calculate the new break-even level of output.
questions.solution: New contribution per unit $= 30 - 10 = £20$. Break-even $= 6000 \div 20 = 300$ units, down from 400. A higher price means each sale covers more fixed cost, so fewer sales are needed; the risk is that fewer customers buy at £30.

questions.prompt: A business borrows £10 000 and repays £11 500 in total over two years. Calculate the total interest as a percentage of the amount borrowed.
questions.solution: Interest $=$ total repayment $-$ amount borrowed $= 11\,500 - 10\,000 = £1500$. As a percentage of the loan: $1500 \div 10\,000 \times 100 = 15\%$.

questions.prompt: A business sells at £8 per unit with a variable cost of £3 per unit and fixed costs of £4000. It sells 1200 units. Calculate its profit.
questions.solution: Revenue $= 8 \times 1200 = £9600$. Total costs $= 4000 + 3 \times 1200 = 4000 + 3600 = £7600$. Profit $= 9600 - 7600 = £2000$. Check: break-even is $4000 \div 5 = 800$ units, and the 400 units above it each contribute £5, which is £2000.

questions.prompt: A business has an opening balance of £2000 in January. Net cash flow is $+£500$ in January and $-£3200$ in February. Calculate the closing balance at the end of February.
questions.solution: January closing $= 2000 + 500 = £2500$. February opening is the same £2500. February closing $= 2500 + (-3200) = -£700$. The closing balance of one month is the opening balance of the next; skipping that link is the usual error.

markScheme.description: carried forward as February's opening balance

questions.prompt: Leo's furniture business made a profit of £15 000 last year, but in March he could not pay his timber supplier on time. Analyse why a profitable business can still run short of cash.
questions.solution: Two chains rooted in Leo. Timing: he pays for timber when he buys it but customers pay for furniture weeks later on delivery, so in a month with a big order he has paid out before the cash has come in, and the profit exists on paper but not in the bank. Spending on assets: buying a new machine or a van uses cash now, while profit spreads the cost over years, so a profitable year can still empty the account. Level 3 links both to the supplier going unpaid.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2): points made with limited development, little link to the case
Level 2 (3 to 4): one developed chain, applied to the business
Level 3 (5 to 6): two developed chains of reasoning, each applied to the business and reaching an outcome

criteria.text: Timing identified: Leo pays suppliers before customers pay him, applied to March
Developed to an outcome: cash leaves before it arrives, so the balance goes negative although the sale is profitable
A second cause: buying equipment or stock, or customers paying late, applied to a furniture maker
Developed to an outcome: a profitable year with an empty account, so the supplier goes unpaid

questions.modelAnswer: Profit and cash are measured differently. Profit is revenue minus costs for the year, but cash is what is actually in the bank on a given day. Leo pays for timber when he buys it, yet his customers pay for furniture when it is delivered, often weeks later. In March he may have bought timber for a large order that had not yet been paid for, so the money had gone out before it came in, and although the order will make a profit, the cash was not there to pay the supplier. A second reason is spending on things that are not day-to-day costs. If Leo bought a new machine or a van, the whole cost left his bank account at once, whereas in the profit figure that cost is spread over years, so a profitable business can still have an empty account. Both mean Leo needs a cash-flow forecast so he can see the shortfall coming and arrange an overdraft before the supplier's bill is due.

questions.prompt: Maya wants £50 000 to open a second branch of her successful café. A bank has offered a loan; an investor has offered the money in return for a 40% share of the business. Justify which source of finance Maya should choose.
questions.solution: Choose, argue both ways, name the deciding factor. Loan: Maya keeps full ownership and all future profit; interest is a known cost; but repayments are due every month whether or not the branch succeeds, and the bank may want security. Investor: no repayments and the investor may bring experience, but Maya gives up 40% of all future profit and some control for ever. Deciding factor: how confident Maya is in the second branch and whether she values control; a proven café with steady cash flow can service a loan.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 3): limited points, little application, no real judgement
Level 2 (4 to 6): developed reasoning for the choice with some application; a judgement is made
Level 3 (7 to 9): developed reasoning for the choice and against the alternative, applied throughout, with a justified judgement that names the deciding factor

criteria.text: A clear choice with developed reasons applied to Maya's café and the second branch
Developed reasons against the alternative, applied to the case
A judgement naming the deciding factor: ownership and control, the certainty of repayments, or the café's cash flow

questions.modelAnswer: Maya should take the bank loan. Her first café is already successful, so it produces the steady cash flow needed to meet monthly repayments, and once the loan is repaid she owns the second branch outright and keeps all of its profit. The interest is a known, fixed cost she can build into her plan. The investor's offer avoids repayments, which would matter if the new branch were slow to start, and an experienced investor might bring useful advice. But 40% of the business is a large price: Maya would give away 40% of the profit of both branches for as long as the business exists, far more than the interest on a £50 000 loan, and she would lose some control over decisions. The deciding factor is that Maya's business is proven. A start-up with no track record might need to give up equity because no bank would lend; a successful café can borrow, so the loan keeps her ownership and is cheaper in the long run.

questions.prompt: A business's variable cost per unit rises while its price and fixed costs stay the same. What happens to its break-even level of output?
questions.solution: Break-even $=$ fixed costs $\div$ (price $-$ variable cost). A higher variable cost shrinks the bottom of that fraction, so the answer is larger: more units must be sold before the fixed costs are covered.

markScheme.description: rises, because contribution per unit falls

options: It falls, because higher costs mean the business must sell fewer units
It becomes zero, because the business can no longer make a profit
It stays the same, because the fixed costs have not changed at all
It rises, because each sale contributes less towards the fixed costs

questions.prompt: Priya has opened a bakery, funded partly by a £10 000 bank loan, and is in her first year of trading. Evaluate whether making a profit should be the most important objective for Priya's bakery in its first year.
questions.solution: Both sides, applied, then it depends on. For profit: without it the business cannot pay its owner or reinvest, and lenders and investors expect it. Against: in the first year survival matters more, and survival is about cash, not profit; building a customer base may mean low prices and low profit at first; some owners' objectives are non-financial. Judgement: it depends on the type of business and how it is financed; a business with a loan to repay needs cash and survival first, while profit becomes the main objective once it is established.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 4): some knowledge with little business terminology, limited application to the business, few connections between points, and a conclusion resting on generic assertions

Level 2 (5 to 8): mostly accurate knowledge with terminology in places, sound application to the business though not always consistent, chains of reasoning that connect points, and a conclusion based on sound evaluation

Level 3 (9 to 12): accurate knowledge and terminology throughout, detailed application to the business throughout, detailed interconnected points with logical chains of reasoning, and a valid, well-reasoned conclusion

criteria.text: Reaches level 1: some accurate knowledge, applied at least a little, with a conclusion of some kind
Reaches level 2: sound application to this business, with chains of reasoning and a supported conclusion
Reaches level 3: accurate and detailed throughout, with logical chains and a well-reasoned conclusion

questions.modelAnswer: Profit matters to every business, because without it the owner cannot be paid, there is nothing to reinvest, and lenders or investors who expect a return will lose confidence. But in the first year profit is rarely the most important objective. A new business must first survive, and survival depends on cash rather than profit: a start-up can be profitable on paper and still fail because it cannot pay a supplier or the rent in a bad month, so managing cash flow comes first. Building a customer base often means low introductory prices, free samples or heavy promotion, all of which reduce profit now in order to earn more later. Many owners also start businesses for non-financial reasons, such as independence or doing something they believe in, and for them a small profit is enough. Whether profit should come first therefore depends on the type of business and how it is financed. Priya has a £10 000 loan to repay, so her bakery must generate enough cash to meet the repayments and cannot afford a loss-making first year: for her, profit and cash both matter from the start. A business funded by savings, or one whose owner wants independence more than income, can treat survival and growth as the first-year objectives and make profit the priority once it is established.

questions.prompt: A shop receives stock from its supplier and does not have to pay for it until 30 days later. Which one of the following sources of finance is the shop using?
questions.solution: **Trade credit.** The supplier has let the shop have the goods now and pay later, so the shop is using the supplier's money for 30 days. It is one of the two short-term sources on the specification, with an overdraft, which is the bank letting a business spend more than is in its account. Retained profit and crowd funding are long-term sources.
options: Overdraft
Trade credit
Retained profit
Crowd funding

questions.prompt: Which one of the following is a social objective for a new business?
questions.solution: Using only packaging that can be recycled. The specification splits aims and objectives into financial (survival, profit, sales, market share, financial security) and non-financial (social objectives, personal satisfaction, challenge, independence and control). A social objective is about benefiting people or the environment rather than the owner's money. Profit, survival and market share are all financial objectives.
options: Making a profit of £5000 in its first year
Using only packaging that can be recycled
Surviving its first twelve months of trading
Gaining a 5% share of the local market

questions.prompt: Give the name of the long-term source of finance in which a large number of people each put a small amount of money into a business, usually through a website.
questions.solution: **Crowd funding.** Many people each contribute a small sum through a website, in return for a reward, a share or nothing at all, and together the small sums add up to the amount the business needs. The specification lists it with the long-term sources: personal savings, venture capital, share capital, loans, retained profit and crowd funding.

questions.prompt: In March a business sells £9000 of goods to customers who will pay in May. In March it pays £6000 in wages and rent. Which one of the following is correct for March?
questions.skill: cash against profit in a month
questions.solution: Its cash flow is negative even though the sales may be profitable. Cash flow counts money actually moving in and out: in March £6000 went out and nothing came in, so net cash flow is $-£6000$. Profit counts revenue earned against costs, and the £9000 of sales were earned in March whatever month the money arrives, so the month may well be profitable. Cash and profit are different things, which is why a profitable business can still be unable to pay its bills.

markScheme.description: cash flow negative, sales may still be profitable

options: Its cash flow is negative, though the sales may still be profitable
Its cash flow is positive, because the sales it made are worth £9000 in all
It has made a loss, because it paid out more cash than it took in
Its profit and its cash flow are the same, since both measure money

questions.prompt: A business has fixed costs of £8000 a year, sells its product for £20 and has a variable cost of £12 per unit. It expects to sell 1300 units a year. Its rent then rises by £800 a year. Which one of the following is correct?
questions.skill: break-even after a fixed cost rise
questions.solution: Contribution per unit $= 20 - 12 = £8$. Before the rise, break-even $= 8000 \div 8 = 1000$ units and the margin of safety $= 1300 - 1000 = 300$ units. Rent is a fixed cost, so fixed costs become $8000 + 800 = £8800$ and break-even $= 8800 \div 8 = 1100$ units. The margin of safety is now $1300 - 1100 = 200$ units: a rise in fixed costs moves the total costs line up the chart, pushes break-even to the right and leaves less room before expected sales turn into a loss.

markScheme.description: break-even 1100 units, margin of safety 200 units

options: Break-even rises to 1100 units and the margin of safety rises to 400 units
Break-even rises to 1100 units and the margin of safety falls to 200 units
Break-even stays at 1000 units, because rent is a fixed cost and not a variable one
Break-even falls to 900 units, because the extra rent is spread over more sales

questions.prompt: In June a business receives £7200 from sales and £1500 from a bank loan. In the same month it pays £4800 to suppliers, £2100 in wages and £900 in rent. Calculate its net cash flow for June.
questions.skill: net cash flow from a list of items
questions.solution: Cash inflows $= 7200 + 1500 = £8700$. Cash outflows $= 4800 + 2100 + 900 = £7800$. Net cash flow $=$ inflows $-$ outflows $= 8700 - 7800 = £900$. The loan counts as an inflow because cash arrived, even though it is not revenue and will have to be repaid.

questions.prompt: A business's closing balance at the end of April was £1800. In May its cash inflows are £6400 and its cash outflows are £7100. Calculate its closing balance at the end of May.
questions.solution: The opening balance for May is the closing balance of April: £1800. Net cash flow for May $= 6400 - 7100 = -£700$. Closing balance $=$ opening balance $+$ net cash flow $= 1800 + (-700) = £1100$. The business still has cash, but a second month like May would take it below zero.

markScheme.description: opening balance for May $= 1800$, the closing balance of April

questions.prompt: A business borrows £15 000 and repays it in 36 monthly instalments of £475. Calculate the total interest as a percentage of the amount borrowed.
questions.solution: Total repayment $= 36 \times 475 = £17\,100$. Interest $=$ total repayment $-$ amount borrowed $= 17\,100 - 15\,000 = £2100$. As a percentage of the amount borrowed: $\dfrac{2100}{15\,000} \times 100 = 14\%$. This is the specification's formula for interest on loans; it gives the total interest over the three years, not a rate per year.

questions.prompt: Explain one reason why the objectives of a business in its first year might differ from those of a business that has traded for ten years.
questions.solution: One point in a chain. The specification says aims and objectives differ between businesses. Point: a new business has no regular customers yet and little cash, so its objective is survival. Development: an established business has reliable sales, so survival is no longer in doubt and it can aim for something further, such as a target profit or market share. Outcome: each business sets the objective that matters most at its stage.

markScheme.description: reason identified: a new business must survive before it can aim higher

criteria.text: A new business has no regular customers and little cash, so its objective is survival
Developed: an established business has reliable sales, so survival is no longer in doubt
Developed to an outcome: the established business can aim for profit, market share or financial security instead, so the objectives differ with the stage

questions.modelAnswer: A business in its first year has no regular customers and little cash, so its first objective is simply to survive by bringing in enough sales to pay its bills. A business that has traded for ten years already has reliable sales and customers who return, which means its survival is not in doubt, so it can set a more ambitious objective such as a target profit or a larger market share. The objectives differ because each business sets the objective that matters most at its stage, and what a start-up most needs is to still be trading next year.

questions.prompt: Sol plans to run a mobile coffee van. He has drawn a break-even chart: his fixed costs are £1200 a month, he will charge £3 a cup with a variable cost of £1 a cup, so the chart shows break-even at 600 cups a month, and he expects to sell 750 cups a month. Analyse how the chart could help Sol decide whether to go ahead.
questions.skill: using a break-even chart to decide
questions.solution: Two chains, both applied. Margin of safety: expected sales of 750 cups against break-even of 600 is a margin of 150 cups, a fifth of expected sales, so the chart shows how far sales can fall before Sol loses money, and the gap between the lines at 750 cups shows his profit, $150 \times 2 = £300$ a month; he can judge whether that reward is worth the risk. Changes: the chart lets him redraw a line and see the effect, for example if cups and milk rose to £1.50 the contribution would fall to £1.50 and break-even would rise to 800 cups, above what he expects to sell, so he would know before starting that a small cost rise turns the van into a loss, and could decide to charge more or not to start. Level 3 needs both chains to reach a decision.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2): points made with limited development, little link to the case
Level 2 (3 to 4): one developed chain, applied to the business
Level 3 (5 to 6): two developed chains of reasoning, each applied to the business and reaching an outcome

criteria.text: Margin of safety read from the chart, applied to Sol's 750 cups against break-even of 600
Developed to a decision: a margin of 150 cups and a profit of £300 a month show how much room he has, so he can judge whether the risk is worth taking
The chart used to test a change in costs or revenue, applied to the van
Developed to a decision: a rise in variable costs or a lower price moves break-even above expected sales, so he can change the price or decide not to start

questions.modelAnswer: The chart shows Sol his margin of safety. He expects to sell 750 cups a month and breaks even at 600, so sales could fall by 150 cups, a fifth of what he expects, before he made a loss, and the gap between the revenue and total costs lines at 750 cups shows a profit of £300 a month, because each cup above break-even contributes £2. That tells him whether the reward is worth the risk: £300 a month for the hours he would work may be enough, or may tell him that the van is not worth running unless he can sell more. The chart also lets him test what happens when something changes before it has actually changed. If the cost of cups, milk and coffee rose from £1 to £1.50 a cup, the contribution would fall to £1.50 and the total costs line would get steeper, so break-even would rise to 800 cups, above the 750 he expects to sell, and the van would make a loss. Seeing that on the chart tells Sol that his plan only works if his costs stay low, so he can decide to charge £3.50 a cup instead, look for a cheaper supplier, or decide that the risk is too great and not go ahead.

questions.prompt: Amira runs a gift shop. She needs £8000 in October to buy extra stock for Christmas, which will all be sold by the end of January. Her bank has offered either an overdraft or a three-year loan. Justify which source of finance Amira should choose.
questions.solution: Choose, argue both ways, name the deciding factor. Overdraft: a short-term source for a short-term need; she borrows only for the weeks between buying the stock and selling it, pays interest only on what she uses for the days she uses it, and once January's sales are in the overdraft is cleared. Loan: a fixed monthly repayment for three years, with interest paid on the whole £8000 long after the stock has gone, though the rate is lower and the bank cannot demand it back early. Judgement: the overdraft, because the need lasts three months, not three years; the deciding factor is how certain she is that the stock will sell by January, since an overdraft's higher rate and the bank's power to withdraw it only bite if the cash does not come in on time.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 3): limited points, little application, no real judgement
Level 2 (4 to 6): developed reasoning for the choice with some application; a judgement is made
Level 3 (7 to 9): developed reasoning for the choice and against the alternative, applied throughout, with a justified judgement that names the deciding factor

criteria.text: A clear choice with developed reasons applied to Amira's £8000, the Christmas stock and the three months she needs it for
Developed reasons against the alternative, applied to the case
A judgement naming the deciding factor: how long the need lasts, how certain the stock is to sell, or the cost and security of each source

questions.modelAnswer: Amira should choose the overdraft. Her need is short term: the £8000 goes out in October and comes back as sales by the end of January, so she needs the money for about three months. An overdraft matches that exactly. She draws only what she needs, pays interest only on the amount overdrawn and only for the days she is overdrawn, and once the Christmas takings arrive the balance clears itself with nothing left to repay. A fixed-rate three-year loan would give her the £8000 with the certainty of a lower interest rate and fixed monthly repayments that the bank cannot change, which is why loans suit long-term purchases such as a van or a shop refit. But the stock will be gone by February and she would still be paying interest on the whole £8000 for another two and a half years, so the loan would cost her more in total for money she no longer needs, and the fixed repayments would carry on through the quiet months of the year when a gift shop's cash is tightest. The deciding factor is how certain she is that the stock will sell by January. An overdraft's interest rate is higher than a loan's and the bank can withdraw it at short notice, which matters only if the cash does not arrive on time; if she is confident the stock will sell, as Christmas stock in a gift shop usually does, the overdraft is the cheaper and better-fitting source, and she should keep a loan for a purchase that lasts as long as the repayments.

questions.prompt: Tomas runs a small furniture workshop on his own and has £2000 in the bank. A hotel has offered him an order for 30 tables worth £18 000, to be paid 90 days after delivery. The timber and fittings would cost £9000, which his supplier must be paid within 30 days, and the work would take him two months. Evaluate whether Tomas should accept the order.
questions.skill: a profitable order that strains cash
questions.solution: Both sides, applied, then it depends on. For: the order is profitable, £18 000 of revenue against £9000 of materials leaves £9000 to pay for two months of his labour, and a hotel contract could bring repeat orders. Against: cash, not profit, is what pays bills; the supplier wants £9000 within 30 days when Tomas has £2000, so he is £7000 short in the first month, and the £18 000 does not arrive until about five months after he starts, during which he still has to live and pay his overheads; a profitable order can push a business into insolvency. Judgement: it depends on whether he can bridge the cash gap, for example an overdraft, trade credit from his supplier beyond 30 days, or a deposit from the hotel; with one of those in place he should accept, without one he should refuse or negotiate payment in stages.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 4): some knowledge with little business terminology, limited application to the business, few connections between points, and a conclusion resting on generic assertions

Level 2 (5 to 8): mostly accurate knowledge with terminology in places, sound application to the business though not always consistent, chains of reasoning that connect points, and a conclusion based on sound evaluation

Level 3 (9 to 12): accurate knowledge and terminology throughout, detailed application to the business throughout, detailed interconnected points with logical chains of reasoning, and a valid, well-reasoned conclusion

criteria.text: Reaches level 1: some accurate knowledge of profit, cash and sources of finance, applied at least a little to Tomas, with a conclusion of some kind
Reaches level 2: sound application to the £2000 balance, the £9000 due in 30 days and the £18 000 paid 90 days after delivery, with chains of reasoning and a supported conclusion
Reaches level 3: accurate and detailed throughout, with logical chains and a well-reasoned conclusion that says what the answer depends on

questions.modelAnswer: On profit, the order is clearly worth taking. Revenue of £18 000 against £9000 for timber and fittings leaves £9000 to pay for Tomas's two months of work, which is far more than a workshop run by one person usually earns in that time, and a hotel that is happy with thirty tables may order again. But profit is not cash, and cash is what pays the supplier. Tomas has £2000 in the bank and must pay £9000 within 30 days, so by the end of the first month he is £7000 short, and the hotel will not pay until 90 days after delivery, roughly five months from the day he starts. In between he still has to pay his rent, his bills and himself, with no other income because the order fills all his time. A cash-flow forecast for those five months would show a closing balance deep below zero, and a business whose closing balance is negative cannot pay what it owes, which is insolvency, however profitable the order looks on paper. The decision therefore depends on whether he can bridge the gap between paying out and being paid. An overdraft of around £8000 would cover the supplier and his overheads until the hotel pays, with the interest a small cost against a £9000 profit; his supplier might extend trade credit to 60 or 90 days for a large order; or he could ask the hotel for a deposit of a third of the price on signing and a further third on delivery, which is normal for a made-to-order job and would leave him never more than a little short. If he can arrange one of those, he should accept, because the profit is large and the risk becomes manageable. If he cannot, he should refuse or offer to make the tables in three batches of ten, each paid for before the next is started, because the order as it stands would make him a profit and make him insolvent in the same year.

examTechnique.body:
Section 1.3 is where Paper 1 puts its calculations, and they are worth learning to do fast: revenue, total costs, profit, break-even, margin of safety, net cash flow, closing balance and interest. Write the formula, substitute, answer with the unit. The formula line earns a mark even when the arithmetic slips, and it is the line most students leave out.

The traps are consistent. Revenue is not profit. Break-even goes up when the bottom of the fraction goes down. A closing balance becomes the next opening balance. And profit is not cash: the analyse question about a profitable business that cannot pay a bill is answered with the word timing.
examinerErrors: Calling revenue profit. Revenue is price times quantity, before any costs.
Forgetting to subtract the variable cost before dividing in the break-even formula, and dividing fixed costs by the price alone.
Saying break-even falls when variable costs rise. The contribution per unit falls, so more units are needed: break-even rises.
Not carrying the closing balance forward as the next month's opening balance in a cash-flow forecast.
Explaining a cash shortage as the business making a loss. A profitable business runs short of cash because of timing and one-off purchases.
Calculating interest as a percentage of the total repaid instead of the amount borrowed.
Recommending share capital or venture capital for a business that could borrow, without noticing it gives away part of the profit for ever.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer writes the formula before the numbers every time and gives the unit with the answer. It chains calculations when the question does, working out a new break-even and then a new margin of safety, and turns the numbers into a sentence about risk. It reads a change off the break-even formula rather than guessing. On cash it explains timing and one-off spending, and says what a cash-flow forecast is for. On finance it asks owe or share, checks whether the business has the cash flow to repay, and names that as the deciding factor.
